summary: Treat a single item and a group of items through one interface.

body:
Rule. Composite lets clients treat leaves and groups uniformly via a shared component interface. A composite stores children and forwards operations such as price or render to them. Trees of parts become natural: folders of files, menus of menu items, bundles of products.

Why it matters. Writing separate code paths for "one thing" versus "many things" duplicates logic. Composite removes that branch at the call site. Misuse builds deep trees where a flat list was enough.

Worked example. ProductComponent has price(). SkuLeaf("widget") returns 10. BoxComposite holds two widgets and a SkuLeaf("shipping") of 5; box.price sums children to 25. Nested boxes work the same because each child answers price. File system: FileLeaf.size returns byte length; FolderComposite.size sums children. Client code prints total = root.price() without caring whether root is a leaf or a box. Drawing apps use GroupComposite of ShapeLeaf circles and squares with the same draw call.  Walk one concrete path with numbers before generalizing. Keep the tone focused and honest.  Walk one concrete path with numbers before generalizing. Keep the tone focused and honest. When to use. Use composite for hierarchies that truly nest: UI scene graphs, file trees, product bundles, organization charts of identical operations.

When to refuse. Refuse composite when the domain is a flat list without nesting. Refuse forcing unrelated types into one interface just to reuse a loop. Refuse composites that hide expensive whole-tree walks on hot paths without caching. Refuse using composite when a simple array plus a reduce is clearer.
